chunks: "I think of it as two independent halves, transmit and receive, each with a shift register and a timer running at the baud rate.
On transmit, software writes a byte into the data register.

The UART loads it into a shift register and sends a frame: pull the line low for one bit time for the start bit, shift out the data bits least-significant-bit first, add a parity bit if it's enabled, then drive the line high for one or two stop bits.
Then it's idle, high, until the next byte. Receive is the harder half, because there's no clock to follow. The receiver watches the line for a falling edge.
When it sees one, it starts counting. It waits half a bit time to land in the middle of the start bit and checks it's still low, so a glitch doesn't count.
Then it samples once per bit time, so each sample lands in the middle of a data bit, where the signal is most stable.
The bits shift into a register, it checks parity if enabled, checks the stop bit is high, and then sets a flag so the CPU can read the byte.
If the stop bit isn't high you get a framing error, which usually means the baud rates don't match.
If the CPU doesn't read the byte before the next one arrives, you get an overrun."
